questions.question: Which way do you want to run the spec-first reset?

options.label: In-repo, gated (Recommended)
options.description: Keep one repo. Cut release/0.33.x for fixes only. On master, each operation gets its observable spec, model and conformance cells before any backend beyond Memory moves onto the kernel. Tooling, backlog and history stay together.

options.label: Fork, spec-only
options.description: Freeze this repo at v0.33.0 and do mostly spec work in a fork. Clean break and no old-spec baggage, but backlog, CI and tooling are duplicated and specs go long stretches without code to check them.

options.label: In-repo, no gate
options.description: Carry on as now with RFC-0017's D3 steps and new specs alongside. Least disruption, but nothing stops implementation from running ahead of the specs.

questions.question: May the new observable-semantics specs change the public Store API's behaviour relative to 0.33?

options.label: Yes, toward v1 (Recommended)
options.description: Specs define the target semantics. Where 0.33 behaves differently, that's a recorded breaking change for v1. Gives the spec work real freedom, and every break needs a migration note.

options.label: Signatures fixed only
options.description: Method names and signatures stay as in 0.33, but observable behaviour (errors, stream lifetime, consistency) may change. A middle path: user code still compiles but may behave differently.

options.label: Describe 0.33 as is
options.description: Specs formalize today's behaviour and record mismatches as bugs. Safest for users, but it bakes in design decisions you want to revisit.

questions.question: During the spec-first phase, which evidence is allowed?

options.label: Models, spikes, probes (Recommended)
options.description: Formal models (Alloy, Lean, Dafny, TLA+), executable reference models with property tests, and live backend probes, as in PR 1173. No production kernel or driver code.

options.label: Formal models only
options.description: Proofs and model checking only, no executable spikes or backend probes. Purest, but nothing grounds the specs in real backend behaviour.

options.label: Plus Memory reference
options.description: Also keep the Memory driver on the kernel as a living reference that each spec is checked against. Closest to an oracle, but production code keeps moving.

questions.question: What happens to specs 001 to 050 during the reset?

options.label: Superseded per section (Recommended)
options.description: They stay in force as the description of current behaviour. Each new spec names which old sections it supersedes, and those are retired when the new one is accepted. No gap in coverage.

options.label: Frozen as legacy
options.description: All marked legacy and describing 0.33 only, with no further edits. New specs start from a clean slate in a separate series. Clean, but two spec sets coexist.

options.label: Inventory, then rewrite
options.description: Treated as an inventory of decisions to harvest, then removed once the new specs cover them. Most radical; history stays in git only.

questions.question: Where should the spec-first work live?

options.label: Master + 0.33.x branch (Recommended)
options.description: Freeze on release/0.33.x for fixes only; the spec work runs on master. One backlog, one CI, one tooling stack.

options.label: Fork
options.description: This repo stays at v0.33.0 and the spec work moves to a fork. Clean break; the sdd/ tooling, backlog and CI have to be carried over and then kept in sync or abandoned.

options.label: Decide in the RFC
options.description: Leave it open now and let the RFC compare the options with their costs.

questions.question: In what order should the specs be built?

options.label: read() slice first (Recommended)
options.description: Spec read() end to end first: the parts of keys, errors and resource lifecycle it needs, its call contract, stream lifecycle and consistency. That proves the method on one operation before scaling; the shared layers grow from real need.

options.label: Foundations first
options.description: Finish the shared layers first (key model from PR 1173, error model, resource and session lifecycle, consistency model), then all operations on top. Cleaner layering, but the shared layers get designed without an operation pushing on them.

options.label: All operations at once
options.description: A call contract for every public method in one pass, then lifecycles and consistency. Fast coverage, but the most likely to repeat 003's contradictions.

questions.question: When may kernel and driver implementation resume?

options.label: Core set specced (Recommended)
options.description: Once read, write, list, delete and metadata plus the shared layers are accepted. Covers what every backend needs, while the remaining operations (copy, move, glob, atomic) follow under the same gate.

options.label: Per operation
options.description: Each operation's implementation resumes as soon as its own spec is accepted. Fastest feedback, but implementation pressure creeps back into the later specs.

options.label: Whole surface
options.description: No implementation until every public operation is specced. Purest, but the longest stretch without real code to check against.

questions.question: Where do the observable decisions (the R-1 to R-6 kind) get recorded?

options.label: Research doc per spec (Recommended)
options.description: As with spec 051 and PR 1173 § 6: the spec holds only the clauses, and a companion research doc holds each decision with the rejected options and why. The interview logs under sdd/decisions/ back them.

options.label: One ADR per decision
options.description: Every observable choice becomes an ADR. Maximum visibility, but likely dozens of small ADRs per operation.

options.label: Inside the spec
options.description: A Rationale note on each clause. Everything in one place, but it mixes the why into the what, which SPEC-DESIGN.md keeps apart.

questions.question: Which backends must the backend-qualified guarantees cover in the first pass?

options.label: Representative set (Recommended)
options.description: Memory as the reference, plus one of each kind: hierarchical (Local), flat object store (S3), session-based (SFTP). Every qualification axis gets exercised; the remaining backends map onto those profiles later.

options.label: All built-in backends
options.description: Every backend's profile stated from the start. Complete, but most of the effort goes into probing rather than semantics.

options.label: Abstract only
options.description: Specs define the axes (stable or not, lifetime, and so on) without naming any backend's profile yet. Lightest, but nothing checks that the axes fit real backends.
